title: Teaching Indigenous Long Island History
summary: Teaching practices that connect Long Island history with living Native Nations and meaningful action.
content:
Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

How can educators teach Indigenous Long Island history without presenting Native people only in the past?

Educators must integrate contemporary Native presence alongside history by utilizing community-authored resources, inviting Native guest speakers with fair compensation, and highlighting continuous sovereignty and cultural survivance rather than treating Indigenous peoples as extinct historical relics.

Educators can responsibly teach Indigenous Long Island history by actively refuting the colonial 'disappearance' myth and centering living Native voices and modern tribal sovereignty. As John A. Strong discusses in 'We Are Still Here!' (1998) and 'The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island' (1997), school social studies textbooks have historically relegated Native Long Islanders to a romanticized, distant past—exemplified by inaccurate descriptions of Stephen Pharaoh as the 'last' Montaukett (p. 45). To break this past-tense bias, educators should utilize primary sources, allowing students to investigate continuous Native agency and labor patterns directly (Strong 2001, p. 214). Crucially, teachers should integrate contemporary resources, such as Unkechaug and Shinnecock Title V programs, or curricula co-developed by Native historians like David Bunn Martine (Jensen 2015, p. 85). Lessons must highlight modern milestones like the federal acknowledgment of the Shinnecock Indian Nation in 2010 and the active language revitalization programs of the Unkechaug and Shinnecock Nations (Strong 2011, p. 31). By inviting compensated Indigenous speakers and framing Native culture as a living, evolving, and sovereign reality, schools can avoid harmful, hands-on classroom role-play while instilling deep respect for contemporary Indigenous communities.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, pp. 6-7, 12, 50-51.
  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, pp. 20-21, 33.
  • Long Island Historical Journal, pp. 212-214.
What makes a land acknowledgement useful rather than performative?

A land acknowledgement becomes useful when it leads to an ongoing relationship and action chosen with the Native Nation being acknowledged. That can include correcting public history, paying Native educators, supporting current community priorities, and protecting land or cultural resources.

A statement alone cannot repair dispossession. A useful acknowledgement identifies the Native Nation or community connected to the place, avoids vague past-tense language, and becomes the beginning of sustained work. Institutions can review whose history they teach, compensate Native speakers and advisors, support publicly stated community priorities, and change policies that affect land, collections, archives, or cultural resources. The appropriate action should come from a real relationship rather than a generic checklist imposed on every Nation.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, pp. 6-7, 50-51, 80-81.
  • John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011), pp. 1, 31.
why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
